subject: Chemistry
description: Major alloys: brass, bronze, steel, stainless steel, duralumin, solder, amalgam — compositions and applications.

options.option_text: Copper and zinc (Cu + Zn)
Copper and tin (Cu + Sn = bronze)
Iron and carbon (Fe + C = steel)
Aluminium and copper (Al + Cu = duralumin)

questions.explanation: BRASS = COPPER (Cu) + ZINC (Zn). Typically 60-70% Cu and 30-40% Zn. Properties: golden colour, corrosion resistant, good acoustic properties, easy to machine. USES: musical instruments (trumpets, trombones, cymbals), door fittings, cartridge cases, decorative items. ALLOY COMPARISON TABLE: (1) BRASS = Cu + Zn. (2) BRONZE = Cu + Sn (tin). (3) STEEL = Fe + C (<2%). (4) STAINLESS STEEL = Fe + C + Cr + Ni. (5) DURALUMIN = Al + Cu + Mn + Mg. (6) SOLDER = Pb + Sn. (7) AMALGAM = Hg + other metals. (8) GERMAN SILVER = Cu + Zn + Ni (despite the name, contains no silver!). (9) INVAR = Fe + Ni (36%) — very low thermal expansion, used in clocks. MEMORY AID: BRASS = BRonze's sibling but with Zinc (B-R-A-S-S = Blends Readily: A Substitute for Silver). ACTUAL: Brass + Zn, Bronze + tiN. PYQ FREQUENCY: brass composition appears in every major competitive exam — SSC CGL, IBPS PO GA, RRB NTPC 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Stainless steel resists corrosion primarily because of the presence of:

options.option_text: Chromium (forms a passive oxide layer Cr₂O₃ on the surface)
Nickel (added for toughness but does not form the protective layer)
Carbon (hardens steel but reduces corrosion resistance)
Manganese (improves hardness and abrasion resistance only)

questions.explanation: STAINLESS STEEL composition: Fe + C (~0.1%) + Cr (10-20%) + Ni (8-10%) + sometimes Mn, Mo. CHROMIUM is the KEY element: it forms a thin, invisible, self-healing PASSIVE LAYER of chromium oxide (Cr₂O₃) on the surface that prevents further oxidation/rusting. PASSIVE LAYER properties: extremely thin (2-3 nm), transparent, very adherent, self-repairs when scratched (in the presence of oxygen). NICKEL: improves toughness, ductility, and high-temperature strength — but DOES NOT provide the primary corrosion resistance. CARBON: needed for strength but HIGH carbon reduces chromium availability for the passive layer (carbon combines with chromium to form chromium carbide) → sensitisation (susceptibility to corrosion at grain boundaries). MINIMUM CHROMIUM = 10.5% for stainless classification. UPSC ANGLE: Austenitic stainless steel (18% Cr, 8% Ni — '18-8 steel') is the most common type (kitchen utensils, medical instruments). PYQ FREQUENCY: stainless steel + chromium in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, RRB NTPC 1-2× per cycle. EXAM TRAP: students say 'nickel' — nickel HELPS but chromium PREVENTS corrosion.

questions.stem: Duralumin is a lightweight high-strength alloy used in aircraft construction. Its main component is:

options.option_text: Aluminium (~94%) with copper, manganese and magnesium
Titanium (~80%) with aluminium and vanadium
Magnesium (~85%) with zinc and manganese (not this)
Copper (~60%) with aluminium and silicon (not this)

questions.explanation: DURALUMIN = Aluminium (Al, ~94%) + Copper (Cu, ~4%) + Manganese (Mn, ~0.5%) + Magnesium (Mg, ~0.5%). Properties: HIGH STRENGTH-TO-WEIGHT RATIO (strong but light), machinable. USES: aircraft fuselage, wings, spacecraft structures, bicycle frames, blimps. NAMED AFTER: Düren, Germany (where it was developed by Alfred Wilm in 1906). TITANIUM ALLOYS: Ti + Al + V — also used in aerospace but more expensive; not called duralumin. MAGNESIUM ALLOYS: Elektron alloys — even lighter than duralumin but less strong. WHY ALUMINIUM BASE? Al density = 2.7 g/cm³ vs iron 7.9 g/cm³ — Al is ~3× lighter. Adding copper + heat treatment increases strength dramatically (precipitation hardening). PRECIPITATION HARDENING: heating then rapid cooling then aging → copper atoms cluster at crystal boundaries → block dislocation movement → stronger. UPSC ANGLE: India's aerospace sector (HAL, ISRO) uses duralumin alloys extensively — relevant for UPSC Science & Tech and IBPS GA. PYQ FREQUENCY: duralumin composition in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC GA 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Solder, used to join electrical components, is an alloy of:

options.option_text: Lead and tin (Pb + Sn — traditional solder; melts at ~183°C)
Lead and zinc (Pb + Zn — used in galvanising not soldering)
Copper and tin (Cu + Sn = bronze — higher melting point)
Bismuth and tin (Bi + Sn = low-melt alloy, not standard solder)

questions.explanation: SOLDER (traditional) = LEAD (Pb) + TIN (Sn). Common ratio: 60% Sn + 40% Pb (eutectic solder, melts at 183°C). Low melting point essential — must melt to flow into joints but not damage nearby components. EUTECTIC ALLOY: an alloy with the lowest possible melting point for that combination. LEAD-FREE SOLDER (modern): due to health/environmental concerns about lead, RoHS directive (Europe) mandates lead-free solder. Modern alternatives: SAC alloy (Sn + Ag (silver) + Cu), Sn + Bi. DENTAL AMALGAM: Hg (mercury) + Ag + Sn + Zn + Cu — used in tooth fillings (being phased out due to mercury toxicity). WOODS METAL: Bi + Pb + Sn + Cd — extremely low melting point (~70°C) — used in fire sprinkler heads. UPSC ANGLE: Lead-free solder regulation connects to global environmental treaties (Minamata Convention on Mercury). RoHS directive affects Indian electronics exports to EU. PYQ FREQUENCY: solder composition appears in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Chemistry GA, RRB NTPC 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Despite its name, 'German Silver' contains no silver. Its actual composition is:

options.option_text: Copper + zinc + nickel (Cu + Zn + Ni — silver-coloured but no Ag)
Iron + chromium + nickel (Fe + Cr + Ni = stainless steel, not German silver)
Aluminium + zinc + tin (Al + Zn + Sn = pewter-type, not German silver)
Lead + tin + bismuth (Pb + Sn + Bi = solder variant, not German silver)

questions.explanation: GERMAN SILVER (also called NICKEL SILVER or ALPACA): Cu (~60%) + Zn (~20%) + Ni (~20%). SILVER-WHITE APPEARANCE — resembles silver, hence the misleading name. Actually contains NO SILVER (Ag). USES: jewellery, cutlery (EPNS — electroplated nickel silver), musical instruments (flute keys), medical instruments. EPNS (Electroplated Nickel Silver) = German silver coated with a thin layer of actual silver. COMPARISON: BRASS = Cu + Zn (no Ni, yellowish). GERMAN SILVER = Cu + Zn + Ni (silverish). STAINLESS STEEL = Fe + Cr + Ni (silverish but ferromagnetic). CUPRO-NICKEL (used in Indian coins): Cu + Ni (no Zn). Indian coins (1, 2, 5 rupee) = ferrite stainless steel or nickel brass depending on year. EXAM NICHE: 'German Silver has no silver' is a classic examiner favourite — testing whether students know the actual composition vs the misleading name. PYQ FREQUENCY: German silver composition in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC Prelims 1-2× per decade. MEMORY: 'Germa-N-Silver = No silver; it's German's Nickel!'

questions.stem: An amalgam is a special class of alloy that always contains:

options.option_text: Mercury (Hg) as one of the components — amalgam = Hg-based alloy
Gold (Au) as the base metal — for dental and jewellery use
Silver (Ag) as the primary component with other metals
Two or more noble metals only (Pt, Au, Ag) (not this)

questions.explanation: AMALGAM = an alloy in which MERCURY (Hg) is one of the metals. Mercury is liquid at room temperature and dissolves (amalgamates) other metals into it. TYPES: (1) DENTAL AMALGAM: Hg + Ag + Sn + Zn + Cu — used as tooth filling material for decades. Being phased out due to Minamata Convention (2013) on mercury pollution. (2) SODIUM AMALGAM (Na-Hg): used in the chlor-alkali process to produce NaOH. (3) GOLD AMALGAM: used historically for gold recovery from ores (now banned in many countries due to Hg pollution). (4) ZINC AMALGAM: used in Daniell cell and Weston cell electrodes. PROPERTIES: Mercury-based alloys are unusual as they can be liquid or paste at room temperature → easy application. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT: Mercury bioaccumulates in food chains (fish → humans → Minamata disease). Minamata, Japan (1950s) — industrial Hg discharge caused severe neurological disease. UPSC ANGLE: Minamata Convention, mercury in global food safety, India's phasing out of mercury thermometers. PYQ FREQUENCY: amalgam = mercury alloy in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, IBPS GA 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Nichrome, used in electrical heating elements, is valued for its:

options.option_text: High electrical resistance and oxidation resistance at high temperatures (Ni + Cr alloy)
Extremely low electrical resistance and high conductivity (like copper)
Magnetic properties and ferromagnetic behaviour under heat (not this)
Lightweight and flexibility for use in wiring of electronic circuits (not this)

questions.explanation: NICHROME = Nickel (Ni, ~80%) + Chromium (Cr, ~20%) alloy. KEY PROPERTY 1: HIGH ELECTRICAL RESISTANCE — when current flows through a high-resistance wire, electrical energy converts to HEAT (Joule heating, P = I²R). Higher R → more heat per ampere. KEY PROPERTY 2: OXIDATION RESISTANCE at high temperatures — Cr₂O₃ passive layer (same mechanism as stainless steel) prevents the wire from burning up even when red-hot (can reach 1200°C). USES: electric toasters, electric irons, hair dryers, furnace heating coils, resistance wires in labs. WHY NOT COPPER? Copper has very LOW resistance → little heat generated, and copper OXIDISES (burns) at high temperatures. LOW RESISTANCE MYTH: heating elements NEED HIGH resistance, not low. UPSC/SSC ANGLE: Joule's Law of heating (P = I²Rt, H = I²Rt) — Nichrome is the standard textbook example. PYQ FREQUENCY: Nichrome uses and properties in SSC CGL, CBSE Science, RRB NTPC 1× per cycle. MEMORY AID: 'NiChrome = Nickel + Chrome = heat-resistant and high-R = Nice for heaters.'
